Heritage walk in Mumbai: Fort, caves and old neighbourhoods

A heritage walk in Mumbai usually covers the Fort precinct and its Victorian Gothic buildings, the Art Deco fronts of Marine Drive and the Oval, and Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus. Older layers sit at Banganga Tank, the Elephanta and Kanheri caves, and the temple streets of Bhuleshwar.

We arrange heritage walks in Mumbai on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, led by an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi.

Why Mumbai matters for Indian heritage

Mumbai holds two UNESCO World Heritage Sites inside the city limits and a third just offshore. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus was inscribed in 2004, the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai in 2018, and the Elephanta Caves in 1987. Few cities let a student stand in front of a sixth century rock-cut shrine in the morning and a 1930s cinema in the afternoon.

The city is also a good place to see how heritage is argued over. Fort's office buildings are still in daily use, Banganga is a working tank with a neighbourhood around it, and the Art Deco blocks along Marine Drive are private homes. A walk here is as much about who uses old buildings today as about who built them.

Layers of history: from island caves to a colonial port

The oldest monuments are Buddhist. Kanheri, in what is now Sanjay Gandhi National Park, has more than a hundred excavated caves cut from roughly the 1st century BCE to about the 10th century CE, with inscriptions naming donors, monks and traders. Elephanta's great cave, with the three-headed Mahesamurti (Sadashiva) image, is usually dated to the 6th century CE. Both are covered in our guide to Buddhist and rock-cut caves in India.

Before the British, the seven islands were held by local rulers, then by the Gujarat Sultanate, and from 1534 by the Portuguese. Bombay passed to England in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's marriage treaty with Charles II and was leased to the East India Company in 1668. Banganga Tank, rebuilt in its present form in the 18th century, belongs to the older Walkeshwar temple settlement on Malabar Hill.

The city that most visitors see is 19th and 20th century. After the old fort walls came down in the 1860s, Governor Bartle Frere's administration laid out a new civic centre in Gothic Revival style: the University buildings, the High Court, and later the Victoria Terminus (now CSMT, completed 1888). Across the Oval, the reclaimed land of Backbay was built up in the 1930s with Art Deco apartment blocks and cinemas such as the Eros and Regal.

Places a heritage walk in Mumbai covers

  1. Gateway of India 1911 to 1924

    Indo-Saracenic arch on the Apollo Bunder waterfront, built to mark the royal visit of 1911. Look at the Gujarati-style jali work in basalt.

  2. Elphinstone College and David Sassoon Library 1870s

    Two Gothic Revival buildings on Kala Ghoda; the library facade has carved portraits and a quiet reading garden behind.

  3. Kala Ghoda precinct Late 19th century

    Named after a vanished equestrian statue; a cluster of galleries, institutes and the Jehangir Art Gallery.

  4. University of Mumbai and Rajabai Tower 1869 to 1878

    George Gilbert Scott's design, with the clock tower facing the Oval. Seen best from the Oval Maidan.

  5. Bombay High Court 1878

    Long Gothic block with carved capitals, some of them comic, by local stone carvers.

  6. Oval Maidan Laid out in the 19th century

    Stand in the middle to see Gothic buildings on one side and Art Deco on the other: the core of the 2018 UNESCO inscription.

  7. Marine Drive Art Deco blocks 1930s

    Curved balconies, porthole windows and stepped parapets in reinforced concrete on reclaimed land.

  8. Eros and Regal cinemas 1933 and 1938

    Two Art Deco cinemas that show how the style reached ordinary entertainment.

  9. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus 1878 to 1888

    F. W. Stevens's railway headquarters and a working station; UNESCO site since 2004.

  10. Flora Fountain and Hutatma Chowk 1864

    The fountain marks the site of the old Church Gate of the fort; the memorial honours those killed in the Samyukta Maharashtra movement.

  11. St Thomas Cathedral Opened 1718

    Oldest Anglican church in the city, with memorial tablets that read like a social history of colonial Bombay.

  12. Banganga Tank Rebuilt 18th century

    Stepped tank on Malabar Hill with ghats, temples and samadhis, part of the old Walkeshwar settlement.

  13. Bhuleshwar 18th to 20th century

    Temple streets, wholesale markets and chawls; a good place to discuss living heritage.

  14. Elephanta Caves About 6th century CE

    Rock-cut Shaiva cave on Gharapuri island with the Mahesamurti panel; reached by ferry.

  15. Kanheri Caves About 1st century BCE to 10th century CE

    Large Buddhist monastic complex with chaitya hall, viharas, water cisterns and inscriptions.

Walking routes in Mumbai

Fort and the Oval on foot

About 3 hours

Gateway of India → Kala Ghoda precinct → Elphinstone College and David Sassoon Library → University of Mumbai and Rajabai Tower → Bombay High Court → Oval Maidan → Flora Fountain and Hutatma Chowk → St Thomas Cathedral

Art Deco and the terminus

About 2.5 hours

Oval Maidan → Eros and Regal cinemas → Marine Drive Art Deco blocks → Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus

Caves day (ferry and vehicle needed)

A full day, or two half days

Elephanta Caves → Kanheri Caves

Museums in Mumbai

  • Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya. Formerly the Prince of Wales Museum, opened in 1922. Strong in sculpture from Elephanta and western India, miniature paintings and Indus objects.
  • Dr Bhau Daji Lad Museum. The city's oldest museum (1872) in Byculla, with a restored Victorian interior and collections on the history of Bombay.
  • CSMT Heritage Gallery. Inside the terminus; covers the building and railway history. Check visiting arrangements in advance.
  • Kanheri and Elephanta site displays. Small ASI displays and signboards on site; useful for orientation before entering the caves.

Best time for a walk

November to February is dry and cooler, and ferries to Elephanta run normally. Start walks by 8 am to avoid heat and traffic.

What you see on a Mumbai heritage walk

A walk through Fort reads the city like a document. You compare Gothic arcades meant for a hot, wet climate with stone carving by Indian craftsmen trained at the J.J. School of Art, look at how the Oval Maidan separates the two styles, and trace the line of the vanished fort walls through street names such as Rampart Row. Our Fort precinct walk is built around these questions.

At CSMT the focus is on one building: its plan as a railway headquarters, its sculpture, and how a working station of this scale is conserved. Groups who want the station on its own can take the CSMT built heritage visit. For the island, the Elephanta visit looks at how the cave was planned and how the large panels tell Shaiva stories.

Neighbourhood walks are quieter. Banganga has a tank, ghats, samadhis and small temples in an area that has seen continuous use for centuries. Bhuleshwar, north of Crawford Market, is a dense trading quarter of temples, wholesale lanes and old chawls where living religious practice is the subject.

Mumbai heritage walk for schools: what students learn

For school groups the city works as a set of evidence. Students can date a building from its style and materials, find the foundation stone or a builder's plaque, and compare what a guidebook says with what the facade shows. At Elephanta they can look at how a single cave was cut downwards and inwards from the rock, and at Kanheri they can read how donors paid for water cisterns and cells, recorded in Brahmi inscriptions on the walls.

Teachers often ask how the walk connects to the syllabus. The caves link to chapters on early Buddhism, trade and the Satavahanas; Fort and CSMT link to the colonial economy, railways and the growth of port cities; the Art Deco blocks link to reclamation, the interwar economy and modern Indian architecture. A short worksheet with observation tasks keeps younger students looking rather than only listening, and older classes can do a measured sketch of one doorway or window as a documentation exercise.

Planning a heritage walk in Mumbai for schools and groups

Fort and the Art Deco stretch are flat and compact, so they suit school groups of any age; start early on a weekday or on a Sunday morning when traffic is light. Elephanta needs a ferry from the Gateway of India and a climb of a few hundred steps, so it is a half day for older students. Kanheri is inside a national park and needs a vehicle and a separate park entry.

Monsoon (June to September) brings heavy rain and rough sea crossings; ferry services to Elephanta may be suspended. For interiors such as the High Court, the University or CSMT's heritage gallery, permission or a booked slot is often needed, so check before you go. Talaash Heritage can pair a classroom lecture with the walk and send a short reading list in advance.

For a longer programme, the Mumbai caves, city and living traditions journey combines Fort, Elephanta, Kanheri and the neighbourhood walks over several days with an archaeologist.

Questions people ask

What are the main historical places in Mumbai?

The Elephanta and Kanheri caves, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, the Fort precinct with the University, High Court and Kala Ghoda, the Art Deco buildings of Marine Drive, Banganga Tank and St Thomas Cathedral. The CSMVS museum holds many objects from these sites.

How many UNESCO heritage sites are in Mumbai?

Three are in or next to the city: the Elephanta Caves (1987), Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (2004) and the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai (2018). Kanheri is protected by the ASI but is not a UNESCO site.

Is a Mumbai heritage walk suitable for school students?

Yes. The Fort and Oval route is flat, about 2 to 3 kilometres, and works well for classes 5 and above. Younger groups can do a shorter loop of about 90 minutes. Elephanta suits older students because of the ferry and the climb.

Do I need a vehicle for a heritage walk in Mumbai?

Not for Fort, the Oval, Marine Drive and CSMT, which are all within walking distance. You need a ferry for Elephanta and a vehicle for Kanheri in Borivali and for Banganga if you start from Fort.

Which museums in Mumbai are good for history?

Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya for Indian sculpture, painting and archaeology, and the Dr Bhau Daji Lad Museum for the history of the city itself. Both pair well with a Fort walk on the same day.
